::: {.abstract}
**Abstract.** Multi-objective AI planning suffers from a lack of benchmarks exhibiting known
Pareto Fronts. In this work, we propose a tunable benchmark generator, together with a dedicated
solver that provably computes the true Pareto front of the resulting instances. First, we prove a
proposition allowing us to characterize the optimal plans for a constrained version of the
problem, symmetric durations that obey the triangular inequality, and then show how far this
characterization extends to the non-symmetric and general problems. Second, we provide a
constructive way to find all the Pareto-optimal plans and discuss the complexity of the
algorithm: computing the makespan of a fixed list of cities is strongly NP-hard, yet the Pareto
front is computable in pseudo-polynomial time. We provide an implementation that allows the
solver to handle realistic instances in a reasonable time, and that returns each front with a
certificate that an independent checker verifies; the central results, the checker and a solver
are formally verified in Lean 4. We validate the solver and the theory in a seeded experiment
campaign against exhaustive searches written independently. Finally, as a practical
demonstration, we used this solver to find the Pareto-optimal plans between the two largest
airports in the world, considering eleven large intermediate airports, spherical distances
between airports and a made-up cost.
:::

## Introduction {#sec-intro}

The progress of algorithmics, the availability of more & more data and the dramatic increase of
computational power drive a fast-pace evolution of the artificial intelligence (AI) field. As
part of this change, the need to assess the performances of computational methods and to compare
their merits is crucial. Many of the core fields of AI have set up standard benchmarks and
competitions, in order to complement expert knowledge and analysis. In that regard, the automated
planning community is at the edge of the state of the art, with the well-known International
Planning Competition (IPC), hosting a large benchmark and using a common definition language.

A deterministic planning problem consists in selecting a sequence of actions (a plan) having an
effect on a state, so that applying the plan on an initial state allows to reach a goal (partial)
state, while optimizing a function of the plan's value. This function is generally the total
duration to reach the goal (the *makespan*), each action having a duration. However, the value
function may very well represent another aspect of the problem, such as the cost of the plan, the
energy it requires or the uncertainty produced by the actions.

In realistic problems, it is very often the case that several such *objective functions* exist
and are contradictory. For example, a short plan may be costly, while a cheap plan may take a long
time. In such a setting, using a linear combination of those objective functions falls back to
introducing a bias about the preferences of the operational user. However, preferences cannot
always be modelled easily in practice, e.g. the user may decide based on political information.
In addition, the knowledge of the feasible compromises between the objectives may, in fact,
influence the decision maker simply because it gives additional information about the problem
itself. For instance, if the two objectives are a cost and a risk, the decision maker might revise
its risk appetite knowing that the increase of the risk by 1% beyond its initial acceptable risk
threshold can lead to a 50% cost decrease.

This calls for the use of multi-objective optimization, where the problem is actually modelled
with several objective functions, and the output of the solver is a set of solutions that are
non-dominated by other solutions, regarding the objectives. The weak dominance of a
$d$-dimensional point $\vec a$ over point $\vec b$ is defined as
$\vec a \preceq \vec b \iff a_j \le b_j$ for $j = 1, \dots, d$. A set of points $P \subseteq X$ is
then defined as Pareto-optimal if every point of $X$ is weakly dominated by a point of $P$, all
its points being non-dominated by each other. The output of solving such a problem is thus a set
of solutions ordered as a "Pareto front". That is, for a problem with two objective functions, a
set of points ordered along a monotonic function. Operationally, the user is still in charge of
taking the final decision, but the complexity of their decision has been drastically reduced to a
$d-1$ dimensional problem.

While real-world problems are often multi-objective in nature, few works actually consider their
study in the automated planning area. The well known IPC does not propose benchmarks for such
problems [[VCM18](#ref-VCM18), [CP19](#ref-CP19)] to this date. In fact, PDDL 3.0 explicitly
offered hooks for several objectives [[GHL+09](#ref-GHL09)], but the only organized competition
tracks concerned aggregated objectives, tracks which were canceled in 2011.

Despite various work on benchmark generation [[LDG+18](#ref-LDG18), [ADE+20](#ref-ADE20),
[BF22](#ref-BF22)] and extension to other planning problems [[PF21](#ref-PF21)], no truly
multi-objective planning problem has been proposed apart from our line of work.

### Previous Works {#sec-previous}

We have previously proposed a problem instance generator for such multi-objective planning
problems [[SSV06](#ref-SSV06), [KSV+13](#ref-KSV13), [QS15](#ref-QS15)], extending the ZenoTravel
[[PW94](#ref-PW94)] problem with an additional objective. Such problem sets are crucial for
benchmarking optimization algorithms, especially when the optimum is known, as it allows for a
rigorous comparison of the performances of solvers.

The original ZenoTravel problem [[PW94](#ref-PW94)] involves planes moving passengers between
cities, while taking care of their fuel. Actions such as flying, boarding, deplaning or refueling
take various time to complete, and a plane cannot fly without fuel. The objective is to minimize
the makespan, while honoring passengers' destinations.

The proof-of-concept of the MultiZenoTravel problem is based on a simplified ZenoTravel model
[[SSV06](#ref-SSV06)]. In this model, there are five connected cities (see @fig-instance), planes
may transport only one passenger at a time and there is only one flying speed. The main addition
to the problem is that an additional objective is attached to all actions. This second objective
is either a *cost*, which is additive (each plane has to pay the corresponding tax every time it
lands in that city) or a *risk* (for which the maximal value encountered during the complete
execution of a plan is to be minimized). In this first instance, three passengers can be moved
across the cities.

The second version of the MultiZenoTravel problem [[KSV+13](#ref-KSV13)] builds up on the
proof-of-concept, allows for 3, 6 and 9 passengers, and a 3-to-2 passengers-to-planes ratio,
which makes up for very small instances, due to the combinatorial explosion of the solution space.

In [[QS15](#ref-QS15)], we introduced an algorithm to compute the true Pareto fronts of very large
instances in reasonable time, and the first version of the ZenoSolver software is described. The
article also provides a few typical instances that exhibit very different shapes of Pareto Fronts,
for different levels of complexity. Unfortunately, this work suffers from two unrealistic
assumptions. First, the distances are assumed to be symmetric around the central cities, that is
to say $\forall i, d_i = \bar d_i$. Second, the proof of the proposition which allows us to find
Pareto-optimal plans relies on the following unrealistic assumption:
$$\forall (i, j) \in [1, n]^2,\ d_i + d_j < d_{ij}.$$
In other words, none of the instances generated under this assumption would respect a triangular
inequality. Even if a benchmark does not necessarily have to be realistic by nature, this
particular assumption drastically restrains the extrapolation of the performances of a solver
observed on the benchmark to real life problems.

### Our Contribution {#sec-contribution}

In this work, we introduce a constructive way to find the Pareto-optimal solutions for the
MultiZenoTravel problem. Our first contribution is to generalize from the original symmetric
clique problem introduced in [[SSV06](#ref-SSV06)] to a non-symmetric clique version and to a
version with no particular assumption on the graph.

As a second contribution, we characterize the Pareto front of the symmetric clique problem when
the flights between central cities obey the triangular inequality, as well as under the
assumption of [[QS15](#ref-QS15)]: every point of the front is reached by a plan landing exactly
$2t - p$ times in central cities, and the lists of cities that can be flown, and how fast, are
described by a parity condition on the way they are shared among the planes. This leads to an
exact algorithm, pseudo-polynomial in the durations. For the non-symmetric clique problem, the
same holds when no flight between central cities is shorter than a detour through $C_I$ or
$C_G$, provided the makespan of a configuration accounts for the waiting it may force. We also
show where the characterization stops: with short flights between central cities, and for the
reduction of the general problem to a clique problem, which preserves the front only in some
cases, for which we give exact methods on small instances.

In particular, we would like to insist on the fact that the triangular inequality assumption made
in this paper contradicts the assumption of [[QS15](#ref-QS15)], so that the latter is not a
special case of the former; both are covered here. In addition, even the technical
implementation of the algorithm has been completely revised.

In addition, we present the ZenoSolver, a C++ implementation of the algorithm to solve
MultiZenoTravel. It can output the instance definition in PDDL such that the generated instance
can easily be used by other solvers. We demonstrate how to generate instances with different
behavior by tuning the input parameters. We provide a theoretical and empirical study of the
performances of ZenoSolver. Each front is returned with a certificate that a checker verifies
without trusting the solver, and the main theorems, the checker and a solver of their own are
formally verified in Lean 4.

Although we think that the primary utility of ZenoSolver is to generate benchmarks with known
Pareto Front to study other solvers' properties and behaviors, we provide a demonstration of the
ZenoSolver on a problem using real data. This has been made possible by the extension of the
solver capabilities from the symmetric clique problem to non-symmetric instances. Real data also
come as arbitrary graphs, and the extension to arbitrary graphs is studied in detail, together
with the part of it that is exact.

### Outline {#sec-outline}

The plan of this paper is as follows: in [MultiZenoTravel problems](#sec-model), we define three
versions of the MultiZenoTravel problem, together with the plans and the assumptions.
[Symmetric MultiZenoTravel](#sec-front) is dedicated to solve the symmetric MultiZenoTravel
problem, followed by [Non-symmetric and general MultiZenoTravel](#sec-nonsymmetric) that focuses
on the non-symmetric version of the problem. In the same section, we study how an instance of the
general MultiZenoTravel problem can be reduced to a non-symmetric clique version, and when the
reduction preserves the Pareto front.

In [Pareto Optimal Plans](#sec-algorithm), we detail how to compute the Pareto front and
construct Pareto optimal plans, and we introduce the ZenoSolver, a C++ implementation of the
algorithm, with its certificates and their verification in Lean. [Experiments](#sec-experiments)
reports the validation of the solver and of the theory, its performances and examples of
instances.

Finally, in [Application](#sec-application), we study an (almost) realistic application for
MultiZenoTravel and ZenoSolver using the OpenFlights database to find the optimal routes between
the two largest airports in the world, and [Conclusion and Perspectives](#sec-conclusion) closes
with the open problems.
